newsitem.title: USA: Cataract surgery half as likely among HMO patients.
newsitem.headline: Cataract surgery half as likely among HMO patients.

text.p: Elderly patients in managed care health plans were half as likely to undergo cataract surgery to clear clouded eyesight as those covered by fee-for-service plans, researchers said Tuesday.

The difference could reflect the priorities of both forms of health insurance, one to cap expenses and the other to increase the number of surgeries performed, researchers at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Los Angeles said.

About 100,000 Medicare patients over age 65 were included in the study that measured cataract surgeries, a commonly performed and usually effective procedure that is the government health program's single largest expenditure.

It found those whose insurance was paid on a fee-for-service basis were more likely to be referred, or to refer themselves, to opthamologists for cataract surgery compared to patients administered by prepaid, or HMO, plans.

"Given the discretionary nature of cataract surgery, it is possible that prepaid settings (HMOs) delayed rather than denied cataract extractions," study author Caroline Lubick Goldzweig wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
She said vision clouded by cataracts can damage a victim's quality of life and increase the risk of falls and fractures, but the study did not measure such outcomes.

"This study is important because it alerts us to the need to examine the requirements for surgery and to measure the outcomes of surgery in the population undergoing cataract extractions," Stephen Obstbaum, an opthamologist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York, wrote in an accompanying editorial.
